name: Jennifer Hudson
description: Jennifer Kate Hudson (born September 12, 1981) is a Chicago singer and actress, raised in Englewood on the South Side and educated at Dunbar Vocational Career Academy, who became one of the most decorated performers of her generation. After singing in church from childhood, she finished seventh on the third season of American Idol in 2004 — then won the role of Effie White in the film of Dreamgirls (2006), and with it the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, the youngest African American to win in a competitive acting category. Chicago proclaimed March 6, 2007 Jennifer Hudson Day. Her self-titled debut album (2008) reached number two on the Billboard 200, was certified Gold, and won the Grammy Award for Best R&B Album; I Remember Me (2011) and JHUD (2014) also reached the top ten. She played Aretha Franklin in Respect (2021), at Franklin's own request as the story is told, and in 2022 — with a Tony Award as a producer of A Strange Loop — she completed the EGOT, the youngest woman and third African American to hold all four major American entertainment awards.

name: John H. Johnson
description: John H. Johnson (born John Harold Johnson, January 19, 1918, Arkansas City, Arkansas; died August 8, 2005, Chicago) founded Johnson Publishing Company in November 1942 and built Ebony and Jet into the defining magazines of Black American life. He attended DuSable High School, where he was an honors student and managing editor of the school paper, and worked as an office clerk at Chicago's Supreme Life Insurance Company, where compiling news clippings gave him the magazine idea. He started the company on a $500 loan secured by his mother's furniture, launching Negro Digest in 1942, Ebony on November 1, 1945, and Jet in 1951. Johnson Publishing proved the existence of a national Black consumer market to American advertisers, and Johnson himself became, in 1982, the first African American named to the Forbes 400. CTL's publishing dossier grades his founding claims VERIFIED, and the graph record's sources include the Johnson Publishing Company archives.

name: Johnson Publishing Company
description: Johnson Publishing Company (JPC), founded in Chicago in November 1942 by John H. Johnson, was the largest Black-owned publishing company of its era. From a $500 loan secured by his mother's furniture, JPC launched Negro Digest (1942), Ebony (1945), and Jet (1951), and grew into an empire that included the Ebony Fashion Fair traveling show, Fashion Fair Cosmetics (founded 1973 by Eunice W. Johnson), WJPC radio (1973–1994), and a book division. In December 1971 the company moved into its own eleven-story headquarters at 820 S. Michigan Avenue, designed by Black architect John Warren Moutoussamy and designated a Chicago Landmark in 2017. JPC operated continuously for 77 years and ended in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy filing in April 2019. Its photographic archive — more than four million prints and negatives — was sold in July 2019 for $30 million to a consortium of the Ford, Mellon, J. Paul Getty Trust, and MacArthur foundations and donated to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture and the Getty Research Institute.

name: John H. White
description: John H. White (born 1945 in Lexington, North Carolina) is an American photojournalist whose photographs of Black Chicago in 1973–74 are among the defining visual records of the city's South Side. Then a Chicago Daily News photographer, he was assigned by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's DOCUMERICA program to photograph Chicago from June to October 1973 and again in the spring of 1974. His subject was the daily life of African American Chicago — activism, music, youth, housing, work, worship, and street life — rendered as a portrait of pride, love, and struggle. The work is held by the National Archives (series 412-DA), digitized and free of copyright restriction. White joined the Chicago Sun-Times in 1978 and remained on staff until May 2013; in 1982 he won the Pulitzer Prize for Photojournalism.

name: John Singleton
description: John Daniel Singleton (January 6, 1968 – April 2019) was an American director, screenwriter, and producer from South Central Los Angeles whose work represented the Black urban experience on screen. Fresh out of the University of Southern California's film school, he wrote and directed his feature debut, Boyz n the Hood (1991), an ode to the neighborhood where he grew up. The film made him, at twenty-four, the youngest person and the first African American ever nominated for the Academy Award for Best Director, with a second nomination for his original screenplay; NPR noted at his death that the youngest-nominee record still stood. He followed it with Poetic Justice (1993), Higher Learning (1995), Rosewood (1997), Shaft (2000), and Baby Boy (2001), directed episodes of Empire and The People v. O. J. Simpson: American Crime Story, and co-created the FX television drama Snowfall, returning to the South Central world of his debut. Singleton suffered a stroke on April 17, 2019, and died at Cedars-Sinai Hospital in Los Angeles at fifty-one after his family removed him from life support; sources differ on whether the date of death was April 28 or April 29, 2019, a conflict this record shows rather than resolves.

name: Joe Budden
description: Joe Budden, born Joseph Anthony Budden II on August 31, 1980, in New York City and raised in Jersey City, New Jersey, is an American broadcaster and former rapper. He broke through in 2003 with the single "Pump It Up", which reached the top 40 of the Billboard Hot 100 and earned a Grammy nomination for Best Male Rap Solo Performance. His self-titled debut album, released by Def Jam Recordings on June 10, 2003, debuted at number eight on the Billboard 200. After disagreements shelved his intended second Def Jam album and he left the label in 2007, Budden released a run of independent albums and performed with the supergroup Slaughterhouse, which signed with Eminem's Shady Records and released two studio albums. He began hosting The Joe Budden Podcast in 2015, co-hosted Complex's Everyday Struggle in 2017, and hosted State of the Culture on Revolt from 2018 to 2020. Budden retired from recording in 2018 to concentrate on broadcasting, and he has been described as the Howard Stern of hip-hop.

name: Jadakiss
description: Jadakiss (born Jason Terrance Phillips on May 27, 1975, in Yonkers, New York) is the rapper whose run with the Lox and a sequence of solo albums made him one of New York rap's most cited lyricists. He formed the Lox with Styles P and Sheek Louch in 1994; signed to Bad Boy Records, the group released Money, Power & Respect (1998) and recorded the 1997 tribute 'We'll Always Love Big Poppa' for their mentor, the Notorious B.I.G. His solo debut Kiss tha Game Goodbye (2001) was certified platinum, and Kiss of Death (2004) debuted atop the Billboard 200 behind the single 'Why?', which reached number eleven on the Hot 100. In May 2025 he launched the podcast Joe and Jada (CTL-E-5598) with Fat Joe, billed by iHeartPodcasts and The Volume.

name: Joe and Jada
